documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
66 y/o retired postal carrier, establishing care. Coming from a prior practice; records release signed, request sent.

PMH (per pt and his bottles): type 2 DM for years, told it was not well controlled; HTN; high cholesterol; PAD (had a leg circulation test at the old office, does not remember results); CKD stage 3, followed by labs only; BPH on tamsulosin.
PSH: cataract surgery both eyes; laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair. Years not recalled.
Meds: metformin 1000 BID, HCTZ 25 daily, atorvastatin 40, tamsulosin 0.4 qhs, ASA 81. Takes them most days.
Allergies: none known.
FH: father MI at 68, also HTN, and prostate cancer at 70. Mother T2DM, stroke at 72. Brother HTN and lipids.
SH: lives alone, apartment, single. Quit cigarettes ~10 yrs ago, 30 pack-yrs before that. Drinks maybe once or twice a month. Not much exercise; mostly TV and errands since retiring.

ROS: no chest pain, no dyspnea, no claudication he admits to, no urinary trouble beyond the usual night trip or two. Feels fine.

Exam: vitals as charted, BP up today. Well appearing, heavy set. HEENT: pseudophakic both eyes. Neck supple. Heart RRR, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abd obese, soft. Ext: no edema; feet warm, skin intact. Did not do full foot exam today - next visit.

A/P:
- HTN: above goal today on HCTZ alone. Recheck at next visit with fasting labs.
- T2DM: no recent A1c in hand. Fasting labs next visit.
- CKD 3: BMP with the labs.
- Lipids: fasting panel.
- PAD, BPH: continue current meds.
- Health maintenance: will review once old records arrive (colonoscopy, vaccines). PHQ-2 negative.
RTC 4 wks, come fasting.

Texted this morning about dark stools; came in this afternoon.

documents.title: Gastroenterology consultation
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
Outpatient Gastroenterology - Consultation Letter
Re: Lawrence Leary, DOB 05/18/1956
Date of visit: 03/15/2023

Thank you for sending Mr. Leary, a 66-year-old man with type 2 diabetes that has not been well controlled, hypertension and stage 3 CKD, seen today for maroon-colored stools.

History: For roughly six months he has had episodes of maroon stool, separated by stretches of normal stool. He has no abdominal pain and reports no loss of weight or appetite.

Medications: metformin 1000 mg twice daily, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, tamsulosin 0.4 mg at night, aspirin 81 mg daily.
Allergies: NKDA.
Social: retired postal worker, former smoker (30 pack-years, quit ~10 years ago), rare alcohol.
Family: father MI and prostate cancer; mother diabetes and stroke; brother hypertension.

Exam: BP 145/90, HR 78. Abdomen soft, nontender, nondistended, no masses or organomegaly. Rectal: maroon stool present in the vault, no mass.

Labs today: hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, MCV 92 fL, BUN 29 mg/dL, creatinine 2.1 mg/dL.

Impression: intermittent bleeding with maroon stool and a normocytic anemia, suspicious for a right-colon source; the BUN and creatinine are above his baseline.

Plan: colonoscopy as soon as can be arranged with a split prep; we have him on the schedule for 03/28. He should continue his medications. Please repeat a BMP in a few weeks.

Gastroenterology

documents.title: Colonoscopy report
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
Endoscopy Unit - Colonoscopy Report
Patient: Lawrence Leary   DOB 05/18/1956
Indication: intermittent maroon stools, anemia.
Sedation: monitored anesthesia care.
Prep: good (split dose).

Findings:
- The scope was advanced to the cecum, identified by the appendiceal orifice and ileocecal valve. Terminal ileum briefly intubated, normal.
- Cecum: several small, flat, red vascular lesions consistent with angiodysplasia. No active bleeding at the time of exam. Each was treated with argon plasma coagulation.
- Remainder of the colon normal to the rectum. No polyps, no diverticula, no masses. No blood elsewhere in the colon.
- Retroflexion in the rectum normal.

Impression: cecal angiodysplasia, the likely source of his maroon stools, treated with APC.

Recommendations: ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily for 3 months; CBC in 2 to 3 weeks with his primary care. Call for recurrent maroon or black stools. Allergies: NKDA.

Gastroenterology

documents.title: Acute visit: back pain
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Low back ache going on since around March. Constant, dull, in the middle of the low back. Worse at night, sometimes wakes him. Tylenol and the store-brand ibuprofen do nothing. No fall, no lifting injury. No leg weakness or numbness beyond his usual feet, no bowel or bladder change. Urine stream is his usual.
O: vitals as charted, afebrile. Tender over the lumbar spinous processes. No skin changes or masses over the back. Strength 5/5 legs, reflexes symmetric, SLR negative.
A/P: subacute low back pain, night pain and age make me want to look further. Family hx of prostate cancer in father. PSA today and lumbar films. Avoid the ibuprofen with his kidneys - tylenol only. Will call with results.

documents.title: Results call
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Called pt with results. PSA 22. Lumbar films with several sclerotic spots in the vertebrae. Explained this raises concern for prostate cancer that may have reached the bone, and that we need urology to examine and likely biopsy. He was quiet but asked good questions; mentioned his father. Urgent urology referral placed; staff to call him with a date. Continue tylenol for pain. He has my cell for anything before then.

documents.title: Urology consultation
documents.author: urology
documents.body:
Urology Consultation
Patient: Lawrence Leary, 67 y/o M
Visit: 09/14/2023
Referred by primary care for a PSA of 22 and sclerotic lumbar lesions.

HPI: He describes six months of low back pain, a steady dull ache that is worse at night and unrelieved by over-the-counter analgesics. No trauma. He has known BPH on tamsulosin. History also notes diabetes, hypertension and a recent evaluation for GI bleeding.

Meds: metformin, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, tamsulosin 0.4 mg qhs, aspirin 81 mg.
Allergies: NKDA.
Family history: father with prostate cancer at age 70 and MI at 68.

Exam: Lumbar spine tender to palpation; no overlying skin change or mass. Motor strength intact; sensation without new deficit. DRE: prostate enlarged, firm and nodular.

Data: PSA 22 ng/mL (08/2023). Lumbar spine radiographs: several focal sclerotic lesions. Today: calcium 9.2 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 140 U/L, hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL.

Assessment: suspected prostate cancer with possible osseous involvement.

Plan: transperineal prostate biopsy, whole-body bone scan and CT of the abdomen and pelvis, which we are scheduling. Will forward results.

Urology

reports.text:
Specimens: prostate needle cores, 12 sites (right and left base, mid, apex, lateral and medial).
Microscopic: prostatic adenocarcinoma, acinar type, involving 7 of 12 cores. Predominant pattern 4 with pattern 3.
No intraductal carcinoma identified.
reports.conclusion: Prostatic adenocarcinoma, Gleason score 4+3=7 (Grade Group 3), present in 7 of 12 cores.

documents.title: Transperineal prostate biopsy
documents.author: urology
documents.body:
Procedure: transperineal ultrasound-guided prostate biopsy under local anesthesia, 12 cores. Indication: PSA 22, abnormal DRE. Tolerated well, minimal bleeding. Allergies: NKDA. Discharged home. Pathology to follow; will forward to oncology and PCP.

Addendum 10/9: pathology shows prostate adenocarcinoma, Gleason 4+3=7, 7 of 12 cores. Discussed with patient by phone. Bone scan and CT are next week.
Urology

reports.text: Whole-body planar imaging 3 hours after IV Tc-99m MDP. Focal increased radiotracer uptake in the L2 and L4 vertebral bodies, matching the sclerotic lesions on recent radiographs. No other abnormal uptake in the axial or appendicular skeleton. Expected renal and bladder activity.
reports.conclusion: Osseous metastatic disease at L2 and L4. No other skeletal sites.

reports.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
reports.text: Liver, spleen, pancreas and adrenals normal. Gallbladder unremarkable. Kidneys symmetric without hydronephrosis. Prostate enlarged. Bladder normal. No pelvic, retroperitoneal or mesenteric lymphadenopathy. No ascites. Sclerotic foci in L2 and L4 vertebral bodies. Abdominal aorta normal caliber with calcified plaque.
reports.conclusion: No lymphadenopathy or visceral metastatic disease. Sclerotic L2 and L4 lesions, as on bone scan.

documents.author: oncology
documents.body:
Medical Oncology - New Patient Consultation
Patient: Lawrence Leary, 67-year-old man
Diagnosis: prostatic adenocarcinoma, Gleason 4+3=7 (Grade Group 3), 7/12 cores; PSA 22; bone scan with lesions at L2 and L4 only; CT abdomen/pelvis without nodal or visceral disease.
Stage: metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer, low volume.

History: low back pain since spring, worse at night. Comorbid type 2 diabetes, hypertension, PAD, CKD 3b, BPH, treated cecal angiodysplasia.
Meds: metformin 1000 mg BID, HCTZ 25 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, tamsulosin 0.4 mg, aspirin 81 mg.
Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: ECOG 1. Lumbar spine tender. No neurologic deficit.

Plan discussed at length: androgen deprivation with leuprolide 22.5 mg IM every 12 weeks plus enzalutamide 160 mg daily. First leuprolide injection given today in clinic; enzalutamide prescription sent to specialty pharmacy. Expected effects reviewed (hot flashes, fatigue, bone and metabolic effects). PSA every 3 months; visits every 6 months with interval labs.

Medical Oncology

documents.title: Acute visit: right foot ulcer
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Noticed a spot of blood on his sock about 5 days ago and found a sore on the ball of the right foot. Hardly hurts - he chalks that up to the numbness. No fever or chills.
Exam: afebrile. Right plantar forefoot under the metatarsal heads: punched-out ulcer, clean base, edges callused, no drainage, slight pink rim. Foot warm. Reduced monofilament sensation both feet.
A/P: neuropathic diabetic foot ulcer, right. Worried about depth given how it looks. Referred to ID and podiatry, both asked to see him soon. Keep weight off the forefoot, daily dressing changes with saline and dry gauze, call for redness, swelling, drainage or fever.

conditions.label: Acute osteomyelitis of right metatarsal bone

reports.text: Right foot, three views. Soft tissue defect at the plantar forefoot. Cortical irregularity of the metatarsal bones adjacent to the ulcer. No fracture or dislocation. No soft tissue gas. Joint spaces preserved. Vascular calcifications.
reports.conclusion: Cortical irregularity of metatarsals next to the plantar ulcer, concerning for osteomyelitis.

documents.title: Infectious disease consultation
documents.author: infectious disease
documents.body:
Infectious Disease Consultation
Re: Lawrence Leary, 67 M
Seen 05/15/2024 at the request of primary care.

History: poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, PAD, peripheral neuropathy, metastatic prostate cancer on androgen deprivation (problem list from referral still reads prostate cancer, suspected). Three weeks of a plantar ulcer on the right foot, little pain, which he credits to his neuropathy.
Meds (per referral): metformin 1000 mg BID, HCTZ 25 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, tamsulosin 0.4 mg, aspirin 81 mg.
Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: T 37.2. Right plantar ulcer 2 cm across; a sterile probe reaches bone. Minimal erythema around it, no purulence, no crepitus. Peripheral pulses palpable.

Data: WBC 7,500/uL; A1c 9.2%; ESR 45 mm/hr; CRP 3.2 mg/dL. Right foot films: cortical irregularity of the metatarsals adjacent to the ulcer.

Impression: diabetic foot ulcer with contiguous osteomyelitis of the metatarsal bone, probe-to-bone positive, clinically stable.

Plan: podiatry bone biopsy for culture and pathology before antibiotics, arranged for 05/21. Offloading. We will choose therapy from culture. Glycemic control is important for healing; we defer that to primary care.

Infectious Disease

results.test: Bacteria identified in Bone by Aerobe culture

reports.text: Specimen: bone, right metatarsal, percutaneous biopsy. Fragments of trabecular bone with marrow replaced by acute inflammatory infiltrate, neutrophils, and focal bone necrosis. No malignancy.

Emergency Department Physician Record
Patient: Lawrence Leary, 68 M
CC: vision loss left eye

HPI: Woke this morning and the vision in his left eye was largely gone, which he says was like a curtain had been drawn down over it. No eye pain, no headache, no flashes. Right eye fine. No weakness, numbness or speech trouble. Hx type 2 diabetes and hypertension, both above goal, CKD 3, PAD, prostate cancer (listed as suspected on our record), prior right foot osteomyelitis.
Meds: metformin 1000 BID, HCTZ 25, atorvastatin 40, tamsulosin 0.4, aspirin 81.
Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: BP 170/95, HR 78. Left eye: dilated fundus shows a swollen optic disc, scattered intraretinal hemorrhages, dilated and tortuous veins, and a few cotton wool spots. Right eye fundus normal. IOP normal by tonometer. Neuro exam otherwise nonfocal.

Labs: fasting glucose 220 mg/dL, HbA1c 9.2%. CBC and BMP at his baseline.

MDM: findings are those of a central retinal vein occlusion in the left eye. Discussed with on-call ophthalmology, who will see him in the retina clinic tomorrow morning.
Disposition: home. Retina clinic tomorrow; primary care within a week for BP and glucose.

Hospital Discharge Summary - General Surgery
Patient: Lawrence Leary, 68 M
Admitted: 05/13/2025 via the emergency department. Discharged: 05/17/2025.
Diagnosis: acute acalculous cholecystitis with gas in the gallbladder wall.
Procedure: laparoscopic cholecystectomy 05/14/2025.

Presentation: two days of severe, constant, sharp pain in the right upper abdomen spreading to the right shoulder, with fevers and shaking chills. Background of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, recent right foot osteomyelitis (treated) and left central retinal vein occlusion; also hypertension, CKD 3, PAD, BPH, prostate cancer (suspected per transferred list).
On arrival: temperature 38.9 C (102 F), HR 110, BP 135/85. Marked right upper quadrant tenderness with a positive Murphy sign.
Labs: WBC 18,000, hemoglobin 13.2, platelets 250,000, total bilirubin 1.2, alkaline phosphatase 120, AST 50, ALT 45, glucose 300.
Imaging: ultrasound with gallbladder wall thickening and pericholecystic fluid but no stones; plain film with curvilinear gas in the gallbladder wall.

Course: IV piperacillin-tazobactam, fluids, insulin sliding scale while inpatient. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy the next morning without conversion; gallbladder inflamed, no perforation. Afebrile from postoperative day 1, tolerating diet, pain controlled with acetaminophen. Pathology: acute acalculous cholecystitis, no malignancy.

Home medications on discharge: metformin 1000 mg BID, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, tamsulosin 0.4 mg qhs, aspirin 81 mg daily. NEW: amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily for 5 days.
Allergies: NKDA.
Follow-up: primary care within 1 week; general surgery clinic in 2-3 weeks. Return for fever, worsening pain, jaundice or wound drainage.

documents.title: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy
documents.author: general surgery
documents.body:
Operative Report
Preop/postop dx: acute cholecystitis, acalculous, with gas in the wall.
Procedure: laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
Anesthesia: general.
Findings: distended, edematous, inflamed gallbladder with surrounding omental adhesions; no perforation, no abscess. Critical view of safety obtained; cystic duct and artery clipped and divided. Gallbladder removed in a retrieval bag via the umbilical port. Hemostasis confirmed.
EBL minimal. No complications. Specimen to pathology.

Hospital Discharge Summary - Vascular Surgery
Patient: Lawrence Leary, 69 M
Admitted 11/15/2025 through the ED; discharged 11/26/2025 to an inpatient rehabilitation facility.
Principal diagnosis: infected gangrene of the left lower extremity with critical limb ischemia not amenable to revascularization.
Procedures: diagnostic left leg angiogram 11/17; left below-knee amputation 11/19.

Presentation: two weeks of increasing pain, swelling and redness of the left leg, and a left heel ulcer draining foul material for months. History of poorly controlled diabetes, PAD and a prior right foot osteomyelitis; also hypertension, CKD 3, BPH, angiodysplasia of cecum, CRVO, cholecystitis, prostate cancer (suspected).
Admission: temperature 38.6 C (101.5 F), BP 150/90, pulse 88, RR 18. Left heel ulcer 3 x 4 cm with black eschar and surrounding cellulitis. No palpable left dorsalis pedis or posterior tibial pulse. Diminished sensation both legs.
Labs: WBC 18,000, hemoglobin 12, platelets 250,000, creatinine 1.8, CRP 24 mg/L (normal <5).
Arterial duplex: no flow in the left anterior tibial, posterior tibial or peroneal arteries.

Course: IV vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam. Angiogram 11/17 confirmed occlusion of all three tibial vessels with no distal target for bypass or endovascular treatment; popliteal artery patent. Left below-knee amputation 11/19. Fever resolved within 48 hours of surgery and antibiotics were stopped after source control. Creatinine back to about 1.7 by discharge. Insulin sliding scale inpatient. Residual limb incision intact on discharge; staples in place.

Discharge medications: metformin 1000 mg BID, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, tamsulosin 0.4 mg qhs, aspirin 81 mg daily; NEW oxycodone-acetaminophen 5/325 one tablet every 6 hours as needed, short supply.
Allergies: NKDA.
Follow-up: vascular surgery clinic in 3-4 weeks for staple removal and wound check; primary care after rehab discharge.

Vascular Surgery

documents.author: cardiothoracic surgery
documents.body:
Discharge Summary - Cardiothoracic Surgery
Patient: Lawrence Leary, 70 M
Admitted 05/20/2026 through the ED; ICU 05/20-05/24; discharged home 05/30/2026.
Diagnosis: acute type A aortic dissection with aortic regurgitation.
Operation: emergency replacement of the ascending aorta with resuspension of the aortic valve, 05/20/2026.

Presentation: sudden onset at home of severe tearing chest pain going through to the back, the worst pain of his life. Background: hypertension, diabetes, PAD with left below-knee amputation after a hospitalization for limb ischemia last November; also CKD 3, cecal angiodysplasia, prostate cancer (suspected per transferred list), CRVO, cholecystectomy.
ED: BP 150/90, HR 88, RR 20. Diastolic murmur along the right sternal border. Extremities cool with diminished pulses in the lower extremities.
Labs: hemoglobin 14, WBC 9,000, platelets 250,000, creatinine 1.7, troponin I <0.04 ng/mL.
Chest film: widened mediastinum, enlarged aortic knob. ECG: LVH, no ST or T changes. CT angiogram: type A dissection beginning in the ascending aorta and ending before the innominate artery.

Course: taken directly to the operating room. Intraoperative TEE showed aortic regurgitation; ascending aorta replaced with a tube graft and the aortic valve resuspended, valve competent afterward. Extubated postoperative day 1. ICU through 05/24 for blood pressure control. Chest tubes out day 3. Creatinine stayed in his usual range. Started metoprolol succinate. Ambulating with his prosthesis and a walker with PT by discharge.

Discharge medications: metformin 1000 mg BID, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, tamsulosin 0.4 mg qhs, aspirin 81 mg daily; NEW metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily.
Allergies: NKDA.
Instructions: sternal precautions 6-8 weeks, no driving, no lifting over 10 lb. Blood pressure goal below 120/80.
Follow-up: cardiothoracic surgery in 3-4 weeks; primary care within 1 week; CT angiogram about 6 months after surgery.

Cardiothoracic Surgery
